description: Melanoma is a skin cancer that develops from melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the skin. It is less common than basal cell carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma, but it is more likely to invade nearby tissue and spread (metastasize) to other parts of the body, including lymph nodes and internal organs. It typically presents as a new pigmented spot or a change in an existing mole.
symptoms: New mole, or a change in an existing mole's appearance
Multiple colors within one lesion (tan, dark brown, black, blue, red, grey); some lesions lack pigment entirely (amelanotic melanoma)
Early lesions are typically flat; may become thickened, raised, and palpable as the lesion progresses
Nodular lesions may be elevated, firm to touch, and growing
Can spread to lymph nodes, causing lumps in the neck, armpits, or groin
A dark area under a nail not caused by injury
warning_signs: Asymmetry - one half of the lesion looks unlike the other (ABCDE rule)
Border irregularity - irregular, scalloped, poorly defined, or smudgy margin (ABCDE rule)
Color variation - a mix of tan, brown, black, white, red, or blue within one lesion (ABCDE rule)
Diameter - often larger than 6mm (about the size of a pencil eraser) when diagnosed, though can be smaller (ABCDE rule)
Evolving - changing in size, shape, or color over time (ABCDE rule)
"Ugly duckling" sign - a mole that looks different from the person's other moles
A new or unusual mark that has not gone away after a few weeks
recommendation: See a board-certified dermatologist promptly if ABCDE signs, the ugly duckling sign, or persistent changes are present. Diagnosis requires clinical examination and biopsy.

sources.title: What to look for: ABCDEs of melanoma
